transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): alright everyone thanks for joining, we're gonna kick off, uh, hopefully keep to an hour. This is primarily a technical deep dive, Daniel will lead the perf part.
[00:18] Daniel (Redwood SE): hi! can you hear me? good. quick agenda: continuous batching overview, scheduler knobs, seq packing, kv cache sizing, then quantization tradeoffs and on-prem notes.
[00:34] Alice (Cobalt): yep good, thanks. our main ask is ~12k TPS tokens during peak with p95 latency under 400ms for short prompts, but we have heavy tail requests occasionally.
[00:50] Ben (Cobalt): and we are VPC-only for now; on-prem later. we need to understand how KV cache persists or if it stays in GPU RAM during warm sessions.
[01:05] Daniel: right, key point: continuous batching aims to keep GPUs fed by assembling active sequences until either max_batch_tokens or max_num_seqs triggers. It works best when seq length distribution is narrow.
[01:22] Maya: note that packing heavily helps but increases decoding jitter, and quantization can change token throughput per core.
[01:38] Sofia (Security): quick interjection - from security we need to know KMS integration for private, and how audit logs capture cache eviction events.
[01:50] Daniel: good flag, we'll cover KMS in the private section. Cache eviction logs are in the console now as events, though we can expose a webhook.
[02:08] [short pause / typing noises]
[02:15] Daniel: ok, continuous batching: typical knobs are max_num_seqs, max_batch_tokens, token_wait_ms (how long scheduler waits for more seqs), and pack_threshold. In Redwood's runtime max_num_seqs controls the concurrency of active sequences.
[02:38] Ben: can you remind us the relationship between max_num_seqs and memory for KV cache? like if we double max_num_seqs what happens to KV usage?
[02:50] Daniel: roughly linear: KV cache size ~= avg_kv_per_seq * max_num_seqs. So doubling seqs doubles KV footprint, subject to per-GPU allocation. If you hit memory pressure, runtime can evict older kv entries or reject new seqs depending on eviction policy.
[03:12] Alice: we saw OOM on our local test when we cranked max_num_seqs; is there a graceful throttle?
[03:20] Daniel: yes there are two behaviours: soft throttle where scheduler lowers pack_probability and hard throttle where requests get 503 or get queued at the front proxy. We recommend gradual ramp with metric-based autoscaling.
[03:36] [00:03 background keyboard]
[03:40] Priya (Redwood Solutions): practical pattern: start with conservative max_num_seqs (e.g., 64) and max_batch_tokens tuned from 8192 up; run load tests, collect avg seq tokens and p95.
[03:55] Ben: how does continuous batching affect tail latency for short prompts? we worry about extra wait.
[04:05] Daniel: token_wait_ms is the knob. If you set low token_wait_ms, you reduce wait but lose some batching efficiency. For short prompts we often set token_wait_ms to 10ms and use small max_num_seqs; for throughput-heavy workloads you raise token_wait_ms to 30-50ms to get packing gains.
[04:30] Maya: also the runtime supports priority routing so you can route short prompt traffic to a low-latency pool and long chat sessions to high-throughput pool.
[04:44] Alice: about packing - do we do token-level packing or sequence-level? we have a lot of variable lengths.
[04:55] Daniel: both. runtime does sequence packing that merges multiple sequences into one batch with offsets; token-level packing is effectively achieved by pack_threshold and aligners. But pathological distribution causes padding bloat; the key is to profile your seq histogram.
[05:15] Ben: we'll share histograms. what about KV cache persistence across requests? we expect multi-turn chats where keys should stick.
[05:25] Daniel: KV cache is per-model-session and lives in GPU memory while session active. We support optional persistent cache on a fast NVMe backing store for private deployments, but read/write latency is higher. For VPC-hosted, KV in GPU RAM is default.
[05:45] Sofia: so on private with NVMe backing, do evictions cause correctness issues?
[05:51] Daniel: eviction is best-effort LRU; it only affects speed (you'll re-fetch context) not model correctness, but if your application depends on long context window, you should size KV accordingly.
[06:10] [crosstalk] Ben: what's the recommended max_num_seqs for a 48GB A100 with 8-bit quantization?
[06:20] Daniel: rough rule: for 48GB A100 with q8_dynamic you might fit ~256-512 seqs depending on avg kv per token. For q4 variants you can often push higher (512-1024) but accuracy/regression risk rises.
[06:40] Maya: and that brings us to quantization tradeoffs - int8 / q4 vs fp16: lower precision reduces memory and increases throughput but can alter logits causing small policy/regression. We recommend eval sets.
[06:58] Alice: can you quantify latency delta? like 95th latency change using q8 vs fp16?
[07:08] Daniel: ballpark: 10-25% faster per token on q8 vs fp16; q4 gets you additional 15-30% depending on kernel optimizations. But that's workload dependent. There is also kernel-switch overhead when mixing precisions.
[07:30] Priya: note that continuous batching amortizes kernel overhead more, so quantization gains can compound when you hit large effective batch tokens.
[07:45] [short laugh]
[07:50] Ben: what about fallback policies if quantized model returns low-quality outputs? automatic fallback to fp16?
[07:58] Daniel: yes runtime supports model variant routing: if quality checks fail (we can run lightweight scoring or A/B on a subset), requests fallback to an fp16 model or go to a canary model. There is a cost delta.
[08:14] Alice: okay, on our architecture we route through an internal API gateway. If Redwood runtime returns 503 due to throttle, we'd like clear error codes to implement retries.
[08:26] Maya: we return structured error codes and recommend exponential backoff with jitter. Also we can expose per-route SLOs so you can pre-fail early on client side.
[08:40] Ben: let's dig into scheduler knobs - any specifics on default values and guidance for tuning?
[08:47] Daniel: defaults: max_num_seqs=128, max_batch_tokens=16384, token_wait_ms=25, pack_threshold=0.75. But these are highly workload-dependent. We generally iterate: measure avg_seq_tokens, set max_batch_tokens ~= avg_seq_tokens * expected_concurrent, tune max_num_seqs to fit KV memory, then adjust token_wait_ms for latency targets.
[09:15] [00:02 rustle papers]
[09:20] Maya: can you give an example runbook? like steps to tune from zero to stable?
[09:26] Daniel: yes: 1) baseline: conservative knobs (num_seqs=64), run 30m load, collect histograms; 2) increase num_seqs until kv usage hits 70% GPU mem; 3) increase max_batch_tokens to match 90th seq tokens; 4) bump token_wait_ms to tradeoff latency/throughput; 5) validate p95 and tail latency under mixed traffic; 6) enable persistent KV if needed for long sessions.
[09:58] Alice: do you have tooling to simulate realistic arrival patterns? we saw synthetic uniform load differ a lot.
[10:06] Daniel: yes we provide a load harness that can replay seq arrival distributions and token lengths. We'll run a replay with your CSV.
[10:18] Ben: network note: on-prem VPC peering may add 5-30ms egress; how do we compensate?
[10:27] Daniel: route short-latency traffic to a local pool or use edge placement. Also set token_wait_ms lower for local pools. For egress jitter we recommend client-side buffering and local retries.
[10:40] Sofia: KMS question: for private we want HSM-backed keys and for audit we need to show key unwrap events. is that surfaced?
[10:48] Priya: we integrate with common KMS/HSMs and emit audit events for model loads and key unwraps; those can be forwarded to your SIEM.
[10:57] Daniel: also note during on-prem cold starts model weights are loaded from secure storage; that can cause initial latency spikes so warm instances or pre-warm hooks are recommended.
[11:15] Maya: let's talk throttling and graceful degradation - say you exceed capacity what should app do?
[11:23] Daniel: recommended pattern: degrade to smaller model, use cached completions for repeated prompts, or fall back to business-logic heuristics. Implement circuit-breakers and measurable SLOs.
[11:40] Alice: do you expose cache hit metrics? we want token-level KV hit rate and miss latency.
[11:48] Daniel: yes console exposes KV hits, miss counts, eviction events, and avg miss latency. We can also stream these as metrics to Prometheus.
[11:59] [short pause]
[12:05] Ben: about packing-induced jitter you mentioned earlier - is there a way to pin sequences to a pool to reduce reordering?
[12:14] Daniel: you can set affinity keys so related requests land on same worker; that reduces packing variance and helps multi-turn state. Tradeoff is sometimes lower aggregate throughput.
[12:30] Priya: careful with affinity on autoscaled pools, persistence must be maintained; we recommend sticky affinity with short TTLs.
[12:40] Maya: okay demo note: we'll share a short run showing metrics and a profiler flame for a mixed workload.
[12:49] Alice: yes please. also we want to see the exact eviction behavior under a sustained chat session.
[12:56] Daniel: we'll create a controlled test where we drive long sessions and then spike short bursts to see eviction and fallback.
[13:05] [ambient background noise]
[13:10] Ben: what's the expected CPU overhead for packing/unpacking on host side? we want to size autopilot.
[13:20] Daniel: negligible for small numbers; on heavy packing you may see CPU reach 10-20% on the worker host due to offset computation, but it's usually network/encoder-decoder kernels that dominate.
[13:36] Alice: can you explain max_batch_tokens effect? we have prompts up to 1,200 tokens sometimes.
[13:45] Daniel: max_batch_tokens caps the total tokens in a single batch. If you have many long prompts, you'll hit that limit sooner and smaller num_seqs per batch will be used. For long prompts, you may want higher max_batch_tokens but watch memory.
[14:04] Maya: question from the chat - do we support quantization-aware scheduling? like prefer q8 nodes for specific routes?
[14:12] Daniel: yes route policies can tag model variants and hardware types; you can route latency-sensitive traffic to fp16 nodes and throughput traffic to quantized nodes.
[14:24] Ben: what about kernel-level optimizations for q4 on Ampere vs Grace? we run on both.
[14:32] Daniel: kernels are hardware-specific; Grace benefits from larger HBM bandwidth so you might see smaller relative gains from q4 compared to Ampere. We publish per-hardware profiles.
[14:50] [00:01 cup clink]
[14:55] Sofia: security follow-up - does cache encryption require re-keying on eviction?
[15:02] Priya: cache-at-rest encryption uses KMS; eviction doesn't re-encrypt, it's just removed. Keys rotate per policy.
[15:12] Alice: any gotchas for mixed workloads, like many short chat messages plus occasional long batch jobs?
[15:20] Daniel: yes mixed workloads are tricky: use multi-pool strategy with routing policies and autoscaling thresholds per pool, plus affordances like pre-warmed standby capacity.
[15:33] Ben: request: can Redwood add a metric for packing efficiency (% of wasted padding tokens)?
[15:41] Daniel: good ask - we already compute padding_bloat and can push it to Prometheus; we'll include it in the demo metrics.
[15:50] Maya: ok we'll run through concrete tests. Daniel, can you outline the exact perf matrix you'll run?
[15:57] Daniel: sure: 1) baseline num_seqs=64, q8_dynamic; 30min ramp, measure p50/p95/p99 and kv hits. 2) num_seqs 128/256/512, same. 3) change token_wait_ms 10/25/50ms to capture latency tradeoffs. 4) run q4_0 and q8 variants and compare accuracy on your eval set. 5) repeat with VPC-network emulation adding 10/30ms latency.
[16:30] Alice: sounds good. can you surface raw logs and a small flame graph?
[16:35] Daniel: yes we'll share S3 links with profiler snapshots and per-request traces.
[16:42] [brief pause]
[16:48] Sofia: on compliance, will the private package support local logging retention and audit exports?
[16:54] Priya: yes local retention configurable and exports to SIEM or object storage are supported.
[17:02] Ben: one more thing - if we enable persistent NVMe KV, what's expected warmup time?
[17:10] Daniel: depends on size; for typical chats a warm-up of a few seconds per session; for large contexts you might need tens of seconds. That's why pre-warm or sticky sessions help.
[17:25] Alice: ok let's reconvene after you run the test. any blockers we should know?
[17:30] Maya: only that we need your seq histogram and an eval set; otherwise we can start.
[17:36] [end of meeting recap tone]
[17:40] Maya: recap: Redwood runs perf, customer shares histograms and prompts, Redwood shares quantization doc and demo artifacts, schedule network & security sync next week.
[17:53] Alice: thanks all, that's helpful.
[18:00] Ben: thanks.
[18:05] Daniel: thanks, we'll follow up with artifacts and test plan.
[18:10] [call ends]
notes: Meeting landed on concrete runbook and action items. Emphasis on seq histograms, KV sizing, and progressive tuning of max_num_seqs and token_wait_ms. Security wants KMS/HSM audit events and VPC peering checklist.
